title: Element order and generated subgroups
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Cyclic Subgroups
terms: order of an element; cyclic subgroup; generated subgroup; finitely generated group; group exponent.

The order of a ∈ G is the least positive m with a = e, or infinity if none exists; it equals |⟨a⟩|.

If a has finite order n, then a = e exactly when n | k, and ord(a ) = n/ gcd(n, k).
The subgroup generated by a set consists of all finite products of generators and their inverses.
A group is finitely generated if a finite set suffices. In Abelian groups, the order of a product
divides the least common multiple of the factor orders, with equality when those orders are
coprime. Without commutativity, this product rule can fail. The exponent of a finite group is
the lcm of all element orders.
The exponent of a finite group need not equal any one element order, as S shows. Without
4
commutativity even a product of two involutions can have infinite order. A finite generating
list of positive rational numbers can involve only finitely many primes in all numerators and
denominators, so it cannot generate the entire multiplicative group.

An element g has finite order, g has order 10, and g has order 6. What is the order of g?
(A) 10 (B) 12 (C) 30 (D) 60 (E) 120

solution.text:
60
The order n of g is a multiple of both ten and six, hence of thirty. Also g = e, so n | 60.
6
The possibilities are thirty and sixty. At thirty the power g would have order five, con-
trary to the hypothesis, so n = 60.

question.text:
What is the exponent of the symmetric group S , defined as the least common multiple of all
4
element orders?
(A) 4 (B) 6 (C) 8 (D) 12 (E) 24

solution.text:
Cycle types show the possible orders are 1, 2, 3, 4. Their least common multiple is twelve.
No permutation of four symbols has order twelve, so a group exponent need not be at-
tained as the order of one element.

question.text:
Consider the group of bijections of R under composition. Let s(x) = −x and t(x) = 2 − x, both
of order two. What is the order of s ◦ t?
(A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 4 (E) Infinite

solution.text:
The composition is s(t(x)) = x − 2. Its kth positive power is x 7→ x − 2k, never the
identity. Thus two finite-order elements can have a product of infinite order when they do
not commute; the Abelian product-order rule cannot be used.

question.text:
Which statement describes the multiplicative group of positive rational numbers?
(A) It is generated by 2 and 3.
(B) It is cyclic.
(C) It is finitely generated but not cyclic.
(D) It is not finitely generated.
(E) It is not Abelian.

solution.text:
Any finite list of positive rationals uses only finitely many primes in its numerators and de-
nominators. Products of those rationals and their inverses introduce no new prime factors.
A prime outside that finite list therefore cannot be generated. The group is Abelian but
requires infinitely many generators.
